repudiate

/rih-PYOO-dee-ayt/ - the stress falls on PYOO · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Repudiate means to reject something as invalid or false and to refuse any connection with it.

In the new preface the historian repudiates his own first edition, calling its central claim indefensible.

Example

The novelist watched the film adaptation once, alone, and then set about repudiating it. She had her name struck from the credits, told every interviewer that the movie reversed her book's ending and its meaning, and returned her share of the premiere proceeds. The studio kept the title; she made sure it kept nothing else of hers.

Repudiate is the exact word for what she did, because it means to reject as invalid and to refuse all association — the tie itself is severed, formally and in public. Disown is the personal, family-flavored cousin; repudiate carries the courtroom chill of a rejection made on the record.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disown: To disown is to cut all ties — the personal, family-flavored cousin of repudiate: a parent disowns an heir, an artist disowns a youthful work. Repudiate does the same severing with courtroom chill — formal, public, on the record, and aimed at claims and debts as readily as people.

renounce: To renounce is to formally give up something genuinely yours — a title, a citizenship, a claim you own and choose to surrender. Repudiate points the other way: it refuses what others say is yours or true, declaring the thing invalid or false and severing every tie to it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

embrace: take it up gladly as your own

stand by: stay loyal to it under pressure

Where it sits · how complete the break with it is

question → dispute → repudiate

question vs. repudiate: Question is far milder than repudiate — a hand goes up and the claim merely has to explain itself — while to repudiate is to cast the claim off entirely.

dispute vs. repudiate: Dispute goes further than question — the claim is now openly argued against — but it stops short of repudiate, which casts the thing off entirely and severs every tie to it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back, away

Root — pudi-: of uncertain origin — perhaps pudere, 'to feel shame'

Suffix — -ate: to make or do

Put it together: Re- (back, away) + pudi- (a root scholars still argue over) + -ate = to push back and away. Latin repudium was the formal casting-off of a betrothal or marriage — a legal shove away from oneself. The re- is genuine and does clear work; what -pudi- meant first was fading even in Rome, so learn this word from the shove, not the syllables.

A root even Rome had half-forgotten: The re- is real — Latin repudium was the formal casting-off of an engagement — but what -pudi- meant first is genuinely unsettled: perhaps pudere, 'to feel shame'; perhaps an old word for the foot, a kick of rejection. No living English relative descends from it, so anchor the word to its motion: pushed back, cast off, refused.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / emphatic

Repudiate is rejection with paperwork: claims, debts, doctrines, associations — declared invalid and cast off, in public. Disown is personal; renounce gives up what is genuinely yours; repudiate refuses what others say is yours or true. Unit-mates for contrast: reprove corrects a person and keeps the relationship, repulse throws back a physical advance, repudiate severs the tie itself. Use it where the rejection is total and on the record.
